blocks.text: In sp3 hybridization one s orbital (low energy, spherical) and three p orbitals (higher energy, dumb-bell shaped) intermix to give a new set of four orbitals of the same energy and shape, each an sp3 hybrid orbital, arranged in a tetrahedral geometry as in CH4. Carbon in its ground state is 2s2 2px1 2py1; in the excited state one 2s electron is promoted, giving 2s1 2px1 2py1 2pz1; the four outermost orbitals then mix into four sp3 hybrids, each with one electron. The energies of hybrid orbitals are lower than those of the unhybridized p orbitals. Each sp3 hybrid has two lobes, one larger and one smaller; for simplicity the smaller lobe is usually not shown. The four hybrids of equal energy have a tetrahedral geometry with the carbon nucleus at the centre. Methane is formed by the overlap of the sp3 hybrids with the 1s orbitals of four hydrogen atoms, four sigma bonds from sp3-s overlap directed towards the corners of a regular tetrahedron.

blocks.alt: Orbital boxes for carbon in three rows. 6C ground: 2s with a pair of opposite arrows, 2px and 2py with one up arrow each, 2pz empty (Ground). C excited: 2s, 2px, 2py and 2pz each with one up arrow (Excited). C hybridized: four sp3 boxes each with one up arrow (hybridized).

Bottom: 'Shape of one sp3 orbital having two lobes', a small and a large lobe, and 'Four sp3 hybrid orbitals', four lobes pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron.

blocks.text: In sp2 hybridization one s and two p orbitals of an atom intermix to form three sp2 hybrid orbitals. The three half-filled sp2 hybrids are arranged in a trigonal planar geometry with bond angles of 120 degrees. This explains the geometry of planar molecules such as BF3. Boron is 2s2 2px1 in the ground state; excited, it is 2s1 2px1 2py1; the three outermost orbitals mix to give three sp2 hybrids. One p orbital of fluorine is half-filled (say 2pz), and BF3 is formed by the overlap of the three half-filled sp2 hybrids of boron with the 2pz orbitals of three fluorine atoms; the structure is trigonal planar with bond angles of 120 degrees.

blocks.alt: A 2s orbital plus a 2px orbital plus a 2py orbital on axes, an arrow labelled 'Hybridization', and three sp2 lobes in a plane with a curved double arrow labelled 120 degrees. Below right: 'Shape of one sp2 orbital', a small lobe marked + and a large lobe.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.29: Formation of sp2 hybrid orbitals from atomic orbitals (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.29).

blocks.caption: Electron boxes of boron in the ground, excited and sp2 hybridized states (original drawing after the box diagrams printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: In sp hybridization one s orbital (low energy, spherical) and one p orbital (high energy, dumb-bell shaped) intermix to give two orbitals of the same energy and shape, the sp hybrids, arranged linearly at 180 degrees. Beryllium is 2s2 in the ground state; excited, it is 2s1 2px1; the two mix into two sp hybrids that lie in a line. This explains the geometry of linear molecules such as beryllium chloride, BeCl2, formed when the two sp hybrids of beryllium overlap the half-filled p orbitals of two chlorine atoms.

blocks.alt: Orbital boxes for beryllium in three rows. 4Be ground: 2s with a pair of opposite arrows, all three 2p boxes empty. Be excited: 2s and 2px with one up arrow each, 2py and 2pz empty. Be hybridized: two sp boxes each with one up arrow.
blocks.caption: Electron boxes of beryllium in the ground, excited and sp hybridized states (original drawing after the box diagrams printed in the textbook).

blocks.alt: Top: an s orbital plus a p orbital, an arrow labelled 'Hybridization', 'Two sp hybrid orbitals' pointing opposite ways, and 'sp hybrid orbitals shown together (Large lobes only)'. Bottom: Cl p orbitals overlapping the two sp lobes of Be in a line, with 180 degrees marked, equal to Cl-Be-Cl with 180 degrees.
